analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest Wall Street banks to publish detailed annual reports on misconduct, pay gaps, trading, and fossil fuel financing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote; it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in September 2024 and died there when the 118th Congress ended with just 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the handful of giant banks designated as global systemically important—firms like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America—to file a detailed yearly report with the Federal Reserve, which the Fed must post publicly. The report would have to cover enforcement actions against the bank and how many consumers, employees, and investors were harmed; employees fired for misconduct; forced arbitration clauses; the gap between executive pay and typical employee pay; minimum-wage workers on staff; branch closures after mergers; whistleblower complaints; trading-desk profits; and financing of fossil fuel expansion and projects harming communities of color or indigenous lands. It is an information bill: it creates no new rules or penalties, it just forces the biggest banks to disclose what they are doing in public.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, bank employees, investors, and communities affected by bank misconduct. Today much of this information—the number of people harmed by enforcement actions, the pay gap between the CEO and the median teller, which branches closed after a merger, how much the bank lends to fossil fuel expansion—is scattered across regulatory filings, press releases, or nowhere at all. A single public annual report would let journalists, advocates, unions, and depositors see, bank by bank, who got hurt and what changed. It would also give the Fed itself a standardized window into the banks it supervises.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, bank employees, and affected communities

how_it_helps.text: The Federal Reserve must post each required annual report on its public website, so the disclosures are available to anyone, not just regulators [S2].

Reports must list every enforcement action against the bank or its subsidiaries—including labor and health-and-safety violations, not just consumer protection—and the total number of consumers, employees, or investors harmed by the underlying conduct [S2].

Reports must show the pay gap between the CEO and the median employee, average pay for each decile of workers, how many employees earn the minimum wage, and how bonus metrics and cross-selling goals are set [S2].

Reports must cover forced arbitration clauses used against consumers, employees, investors, and contractors; the number of employees fired for misconduct and whether any were executives; and the volume and resolution of internal whistleblower complaints [S2].

Reports must disclose financing to fossil fuel expansion, emissions targets and reliance on offsets, financing for pipelines and petrochemical plants in low-income or majority-minimum-minority census tracts and on indigenous lands, and branch closures and market-concentration changes caused by recent mergers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The largest bank holding companies, which would bear the cost of compiling and verifying the reports—listing every subsidiary, breaking down trading-desk profits and pay by decile, and describing ten years of changes. Beyond compliance cost, the exposure itself is the price: publicizing enforcement records, pay gaps, arbitration use, and fossil fuel financing invites scrutiny from customers, employees, regulators, and lawmakers. Because the reports are public and the subject matter is politically sensitive, banks would have an incentive to minimize the conduct the reports reveal.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no new rules, penalties, or standards—it only requires disclosure, so a bank can report its misconduct, pay practices, and fossil fuel financing and continue all of them unchanged [S2].

The reporting demands are extensive and granular—every subsidiary, trading-desk inventory statistics, decile-by-decile pay, and ten-year comparisons—which would impose real compliance costs on the affected firms, and critics would argue much of this data already exists in regulatory filings, lawsuits, and bank sustainability reports [S2].

Requiring detailed descriptions of trading-desk structures, inventory levels, and compensation methodologies touches competitively sensitive information, and banks would argue some disclosures could aid competitors; the bill's six-month lag on inventory data is meant to limit that, but the objection is real [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is genuine but modest by design: sunshine without sanctions. Forcing eight or so megabanks to publicly account for who they harmed, how they pay people, what they closed, and what they finance gives watchdogs and depositors real leverage, at a compliance cost that is trivial for firms this size. The honest limitation is that a report changes nothing by itself; if misconduct, low pay, branch closures, or fossil fuel financing continue, the bill's only answer is that the public will now know. As a first step toward accountability, it is a fair trade; as a substitute for enforcement, it would not be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1].
That referral was the only action the bill ever received; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded in its action history [S4].
The bill had 3 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not passed by both chambers expire [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest global banks are better off: they were never required to publish a public annual accounting of enforcement actions, employee pay and misconduct, arbitration clauses, merger-driven branch closures, or fossil fuel financing. The Financial Services Committee majority also avoided a recorded vote on a bill targeting Wall Street's biggest firms.

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole advocate in the chamber.

for.name: 3 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names in support; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-led majority in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, markup, or vote—so it never advanced.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.role: Chair, House Financial Services Committee (118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration; under House practice, a bill does not reach the floor without committee action or a discharge petition that never materialized here.

sides.party_line_note: All 4 supporters—the sponsor and 3 cosponsors—were Democrats, no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired committee never acted on the bill [S3, S4].

industries.industry: Global systemically important bank holding companies (the largest Wall Street banks)
industries.note: The bill would cost these firms compliance effort and, more importantly, force public disclosure of enforcement actions and harm counts, CEO-to-worker pay gaps, forced arbitration use, misconduct firings, merger-driven branch closures, and fossil fuel financing—information many of these banks do not currently assemble or publicize in one place. The banks' interest in keeping that record quiet runs against the consumers, employees, and communities the disclosure would serve.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel companies and expansion projects
industries.note: The bill requires banks to report financing provided to fossil fuel expansion and to pipelines, refineries, and petrochemical plants sited in low-income, majority-minority, or indigenous areas. Publicly naming that money flow would expose projects and lenders to pressure they currently avoid.

industries.industry: Minority depository institutions and community development financial institutions
industries.note: Megabanks would have to report their investments, partnerships, and support for these community lenders. The exposure could push more capital toward them, though the requirement is reporting only.
